No, this doesn't work as-is — it has three claims that overreach what an MIT license or internal testing can actually support.

**1. "MIT license... so it's open and safe for anyone to use in production payment systems"**
This is a non-sequitur that actually contradicts the license itself. MIT is a permissive *legal* grant with an explicit "AS IS," no-warranty, no-fitness-for-purpose disclaimer. Claiming the license makes it "safe for production" reads as an express safety/fitness assurance sitting right next to a license that disclaims exactly that — which undercuts the disclaimer's protection and creates real liability exposure if something goes wrong in a user's payment flow.

**2. "Fully compliant with PCI security standards"**
PCI DSS compliance is an assessment of an entire cardholder-data environment (systems, processes, controls), validated by a QSA/audit — not a property a standalone library can possess on its own. A downstream user could rely on this claim, fail their own PCI audit, and point back at this README. This needs to be scoped down to what the library actually does (e.g., supports/aligns with specific PCI requirements) rather than declaring blanket compliance.

**3. "Passed all our internal tests"**
Less risky, but vague — "all our internal tests" implies more rigor than it likely proves. Fine to keep if scoped (what kind of tests, e.g., unit/integration).

**Suggested rewrite:**

> PayCheck is released under the MIT license. It is provided "as is," without warranty of any kind — see the [LICENSE](./LICENSE) file for full terms. PayCheck has passed our internal unit and integration test suite, but it is your responsibility to validate it for your own environment and requirements. PayCheck is designed to help support certain PCI DSS controls (e.g., [specify which, such as secure handling of cardholder data in transit]), but using this library does not by itself make your system PCI compliant — compliance depends on your full environment and must be validated through your own assessment process.

Want me to tighten this further once you tell me which specific PCI controls (if any) the library was actually designed against?
